title: CSR spending per resident against multidimensional poverty, by state
headline: Bihar received ₹19 of company CSR spending per resident in 2022-23. Maharashtra received ₹436.
sub: Bihar's multidimensional poverty index is 4.8 times Maharashtra's. Maharashtra's CSR per resident is 23 times Bihar's.

pair.label: Five states with the most multidimensional poverty

chart.title: CSR per resident, states ordered from most to least multidimensional poverty

note: ₹7,030 crore (23% of the ₹29,988 crore total) was spent "PAN India" or with no state named, and is outside every figure here. A project is counted in the state the company reported for it.

sources.name: Ministry of Corporate Affairs, State/UT-wise CSR expenditure 2018-19 to 2022-23
sources.detail: Open Government Data Platform, resource 80f3abf8-7c91-4966-a37f-8c7b0aae92e9, 2022-23 column

sources.name: NITI Aayog, National Multidimensional Poverty Index: A Progress Review 2023
sources.detail: Overview of States and UTs, p. 36; MPI from NFHS-5 (2019-21)

sources.name: Technical Group on Population Projections, Population Projections for India and States 2011-2036 (MoHFW, November 2019)
sources.detail: Table 14, projected population on 1 October 2022, pp. 121-136

method: CSR per resident is a state's 2022-23 CSR spending divided by its projected population on 1 October 2022, the middle of the financial year.

States are ranked by NITI Aayog's multidimensional poverty index (MPI) for 2019-21, and where two share an MPI at the three decimals NITI prints, by the share of people who are poor (the headcount ratio). That decides Himachal Pradesh and Punjab.
The five-state figures pool spending and population across the five, so a small state does not count as much as a large one.

The ₹7,030 crore recorded as "PAN India", "PAN India (Other Centralized Funds)" or "NEC/Not Mentioned" is not assigned to any state and is left out. Spreading it by population would raise every state by the same amount per resident and change none of the ranks.
The CSR Explorer divides by the 2011 census, the last count taken, so its per-resident figures run higher than these for fast-growing states.

The ministry records the state the company reported for each project. A company headquartered in Mumbai can report national work as Maharashtra's, so part of the gap measures where companies are based.

title: Undertrial prisoners by caste, against the population
headline: Scheduled Castes and Tribes are 25.9% of the population and 33.1% of undertrial prisoners.
sub: Scheduled Castes are 17.2% of the population and 22.5% of undertrials. Scheduled Tribes are 8.7% and 10.6%.

chart.title: SC and ST share of undertrials over their share of the population, states with 1,000+ undertrials (1 means in proportion)

note: An undertrial has not been convicted of the offence they are held for. Prisoners are counted on 31 December 2023 and people in the 2011 census. Andhra Pradesh, Ladakh, Maharashtra and Telangana are left out (see the working).

sources.name: National Crime Records Bureau, Prison Statistics India 2023
sources.detail: State/UT-wise caste of undertrial prisoners as on 31-12-2023, Open Government Data Platform resource 6e069039-64bd-43da-8f5a-15cb697caf1b

sources.name: Census of India 2011, Scheduled Caste population by state

sources.name: Ministry of Tribal Affairs, State/UT-wise Scheduled Tribe population as per Census 2011
sources.detail: Open Government Data Platform resource a5cd7e55-2e13-4017-9f8c-410dad9cc518

method: A state's share is its Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe undertrials divided by all its undertrials whose caste the prison recorded.
The population share is the state's Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe population in the 2011 census over its total population. The 2021 census was not held, so 2011 is the latest count.
The national figures pool prisoners and people across the same states, so both sides cover the same places.

Maharashtra reported no caste breakdown for its undertrials. Andhra Pradesh and Telangana are left out because the 2011 count covers the undivided state, and Ladakh because it was not a separate unit in 2011.

Scheduled Tribe population is taken from the Ministry of Tribal Affairs table. The ST column of the combined census table on the same platform is scrambled across rows; the Justice Explorer explains how that was found.
The chart leaves out states with fewer than 1,000 undertrials whose caste was recorded, where a few dozen people move the ratio a long way. The table shows every state.
Over-representation among undertrials can come from arrest, from charge, or from who can raise bail. These figures do not say which.

title: How men and women get to work, from the National Household Travel Survey
headline: 61.9% of working men made a trip of a kilometre or more to work on the survey's travel day. For working women it was 41.9%.
sub: Among workers with a fixed workplace, women spend ₹533 a month on the trip there and back. Men spend ₹835.

pair.label: Working men who travel to work
Working women who travel to work

chart.title: Workers aged 15+ who travel 1 km or more to work, %

note: A worker who works at home or within a kilometre of it makes no trip the survey counts, so part of the gap is where women's work is.

sources.name: National Statistics Office, Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, Government of India, National Household Travel Survey, July 2025 to June 2026: Press Note and Factsheet
sources.detail: Table 3 (workers who travel, by sector, sex and age) and Figure 5 (monthly cost), released 5 October 2026

method: Workers are people aged 15 and over working in the week before the survey (current weekly status).
A worker travels if they make a trip of 1 km or more to a fixed or non-fixed workplace on the travel day. Shorter trips were not recorded.
The monthly cost covers trips to and from a fixed workplace only, so it leaves out workers whose place of work changes.
The figures are the survey's own estimates for persons, transcribed from the press note's tables. The survey publishes no breakdown by sex for each state.

title: Dates on the Central OBC list, file year against resolution date
headline: 654 of the 1,070 entries added to the Central OBC list after 1993 are filed under a different year from the date on their resolution.
sub: The gazette file numbers put 115 additions in 1998. No entry's resolution is dated 1998.

pair.label: Added after 1993, with a printed date

chart.title: Share of post-1993 entries filed under another year, states with 20+ such entries

note: The difference is 1 to 5 years. All 1,337 entries in the first list of 1993 carry 1993 in both places.

sources.name: Jolad, S. and Kalyani, G. (2026), Database of castes: SC, ST, OBC and 1931 Caste Census, Harvard Dataverse, V1.1
sources.short: Jolad and Kalyani, Database of castes (2026)
sources.detail: OBC list, with the gazette file number and the printed resolution date of every entry

method: The database records, for each entry, the year in its gazette file number (12011/14/2004-BCC is 2004) and the date printed on the resolution that added it.
An entry counts as filed under another year when the two years differ. 21 active entries print no date and are left out.
File 12011/14/2004-BCC, for example, carries a resolution dated 12 March 2007.

The chart leaves out states with fewer than 20 entries added after 1993. The table shows every state. Every later entry is filed under another year in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Puducherry and Telangana.
A count of castes added each year is right only if it uses the resolution date. Analysis that reads the year off the file number moves the additions back by one to five years.
